speaker: John Jumper
title: He won a Nobel here for AlphaFold. Then he left. - John Jumper
question: In AI for biology, why can building a narrow predictor for one specific experiment outperform trying to model the entire cell?
guest: I think what's really important is almost the humility of AlphaFold: we are trying to predict what this specific experiment will give you. We are not trying to tell you everything. We are not a model of the entire cell. We are a predictor of this experiment that you did all the time and took you a year. Because of that, we have validity—I can characterize very well how accurately we will reproduce that experiment. And then people figure out how to take this machine and use it in ways we didn't expect, like running thousands of predictions to find two proteins that stick together and uncover an unknown component of a complex system. We predict Nature-level science with the press of a button in a very narrow category. The other story of machine learning is that predicting things okay is all right, but predicting things extraordinarily well starts to produce amazing machines. There is an enormous universe of biology where we have to figure out what data to pin ourselves to and what experiments to predict really well, rather than just building one universal biology machine.

points.core: Pinning predictions to a concrete experiment lets you rigorously measure model validity.
points.note: Accept: anchoring to a well-defined experimental measurement or assay so accuracy against ground truth is objectively verifiable. Do not credit: generic praise for benchmarks or evaluation metrics without tying validity to a reproducible experiment.

points.core: Achieving extraordinary accuracy on a narrow task unlocks unexpected downstream scientific uses.
points.note: Accept: ultra-high reliability creating a phase shift where scientists repurpose the model at scale (e.g., screening thousands of protein pairs) to discover mechanisms the builders never planned. Do not credit: generic statements that accurate models are useful.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A narrow predictor often wins because it matches the problem to the data you actually have. A single experiment, such as a specific perturbation screen or binding assay, gives dense, consistent measurements of one well-defined input–output relationship, with the cell type, conditions and readout held fixed. The model only has to learn that mapping, so the signal-to-noise ratio is high and evaluation is straightforward.

A whole-cell model, by contrast, must capture an enormous combinatorial space of states, cell types, perturbations and timescales, while the available data are sparse, noisy, mostly observational snapshots, and riddled with batch effects across labs and platforms. Much of the relevant biology (protein levels, localisation, metabolism, dynamics) isn't even measured, so the system is badly underdetermined. General models then tend to learn dominant sources of variation, such as cell type or technical artefacts, rather than the subtle causal effects a given experiment cares about.

This shows up empirically: in several benchmarks of perturbation-response prediction, large single-cell foundation models have failed to beat simple linear or mean-based baselines. Narrow models also benefit from tight lab-in-the-loop iteration, where new experiments directly target the model's errors.

points.why: The candidate ties evaluation to a fixed experimental readout that provides measured outcomes against which predictions can be checked.
quotes: A single experiment, such as a specific perturbation screen or binding assay, gives dense, consistent measurements of one well-defined input–output relationship, with the cell type, conditions and readout held fixed.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Modeling an entire cell requires capturing vast, multiscale interactions across genes, proteins, metabolites, and spatial states, most of which go unmeasured in standard assays. Whole-cell models must pool heterogeneous datasets across labs, cell types, and protocols, forcing them to absorb severe batch effects, technical artifacts, and conflicting context-dependent biology. Because their training data largely consists of static observational snapshots rather than dense causal interventions, general models often spend capacity learning broad background correlations while compounding errors across poorly constrained pathways.

In contrast, a narrow predictor optimizes directly for one experimental mapping within a consistent biological context and measurement protocol. Holding cell state and assay noise constant sidesteps cross-dataset distribution shifts and avoids estimating thousands of unidentifiable intermediate variables. Statistical power and domain priors focus entirely on the target readout, which is why specialized predictors—and even simple baselines—trained on clean, task-matched data frequently outperform ambitious virtual-cell foundation models on concrete benchmarks.

noweb.answer:
Building a narrow predictor for a single experiment often outperforms whole-cell modeling because it aligns model capacity directly with homogeneous data and a well-defined objective. A single assay generates consistent measurements under controlled conditions, allowing a specialized model to learn the exact empirical relationship—including assay-specific biases and measurement noise—between perturbations and the target readout.

By contrast, modeling an entire cell requires integrating sparse, heterogeneous datasets across vastly different spatial and temporal scales, where batch effects and incompatible protocols distort biological signal. Because most intracellular states, molecular interactions, and kinetic parameters remain unobserved, whole-cell models suffer from severe identifiability limits and compounding errors across coupled pathways. Furthermore, a general-purpose cellular model must distribute its capacity and training objective across thousands of processes irrelevant to the specific experimental question, diluting accuracy on the target phenotype. When sufficient data exists for a particular assay, directly learning the input-to-readout mapping bypasses poorly characterized intermediate mechanisms and yields sharper, better-calibrated predictions within that experimental regime.

The response claims that specialization improves prediction quality but does not explain how exceptional accuracy enables unexpected scientific uses.
The response explains why whole-cell models can be less accurate on a target phenotype but does not link that loss of precision to an inability to guide lab decisions or change scientific workflows.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A narrow predictor usually wins because it fits the data and the goal you actually have. A specific experiment, such as predicting one assay's readout for one cell type under defined perturbations, comes with plenty of matched, consistently measured training data. The labels are clean and the success metric is clear, so the model can learn the relevant signal and be validated directly against held-out data from the same experiment.

A "virtual cell" model faces a far harder problem. It has to represent thousands of interacting molecules across contexts, timescales and cell states. The data it would learn from are sparse, noisy and full of batch effects, and they come from many labs, modalities and protocols that don't line up well. Most of the model's capacity goes into variation that doesn't matter for your question. Errors also compound across a mechanistic chain, and it's unclear what ground truth to benchmark against. Recent evaluations have repeatedly found that simple, task-specific baselines match or beat large foundation models on perturbation prediction.

In practice, a narrow model is cheaper and quicker to iterate in lab-in-the-loop cycles, and it's useful now. Whole-cell modeling remains an aspiration, limited above all by the data available.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
A living cell contains tens of thousands of interacting genes, proteins, metabolites, and spatial states, most of which remain unmeasured in any single assay. Attempting to model the entire cell forces an AI system to infer a vast web of hidden variables from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous data, causing small errors in intermediate mechanisms to compound rapidly and leaving the model underdetermined.

By contrast, a narrow predictor maps directly from the controlled inputs of one experiment—such as a DNA sequence, molecule, or genetic perturbation—to a specific, well-defined readout. Optimizing directly for that target lets the model focus its capacity on the relevant signal, absorb assay-specific quirks and experimental conditions, and avoid simulating irrelevant pathways. Because the problem is tightly scoped, it also aligns cleanly with high-throughput data generation, rigorous benchmarking, and iterative lab-in-the-loop refinement, consistently yielding stronger predictive accuracy than a general whole-cell simulation.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A narrow predictor can outperform a whole-cell model at a specific experiment because it learns the relationship you actually need: how the inputs you control affect the outcome you measure. If you’re predicting how much of a protein a sample will produce under a fixed protocol, training on measurements from that protocol lets the model focus on the variation that matters for that readout. It can make useful predictions even when many of the underlying cellular processes are unmeasured.

A whole-cell model has to account for many interacting processes, often using incomplete data collected under different conditions. Errors in those processes can carry through to the final prediction. A narrow model is also easier to test prospectively: make predictions, run the experiment, and compare them with the measurements. Its advantage is strongest when future experiments resemble its training data. If the protocol or cell type changes, that advantage may disappear.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A single experiment asks a narrower question than “how does this cell work?” Under fixed conditions, a few signals may predict the measured outcome reliably. A narrow predictor can learn from examples collected under those conditions, and its errors can be checked against the exact measurement researchers care about.

A whole-cell model also has to estimate many interactions that are poorly measured or have little effect on that outcome. With limited data, those extra assumptions can add error without improving the prediction. The trade-off is scope. A predictor that works well for one experiment may lose accuracy in a different cell type or under a new treatment, especially if the correlations it learned no longer hold.
